title: Live: Clarkson 'no longer has belief' of club, Kangaroos boss tells media
text:
North Melbourne has parted ways with coach Alastair Clarkson after four AFL seasons.

Clarkson, who guided Hawthorn to four premierships as a coach, has been unable to lead the Kangaroos to the finals during his time at Arden Street.

Clarkson was contracted with the club until 2027, but the Kangaroos opted to end his tenure early.

Live Moment North Melbourne president Sonja Hood and general manager of football Todd Viney address the media after Alastair Clarkson's departure. Hood and Viney are now here Here we go! Sonja Hood and Todd Viney are at the podium now speaking to the media on hand. Hood's letter says Clarkson exit came after consultations Sonja Hood has released a letter to the club's members and this line makes for particularly interesting reading. "...But now, having consulted widely across the club, it has become clear that Alastair no longer has the belief from enough people at the club that he is the right coach to take this group forward." Alastair Clarkson's season by season record Clarkson departs Arden St having overseen four years in charge. There was steady improvement, but not enough for the Kangaroos powerbrokers evidently. Here's his season by season record: 2023: 3-10 2024: 3-20 2025: 5-17 (1 draw) 2026: 9-14 Welcome! Good afternoon and welcome to ABC Sport's live coverage from North Melbourne's press conference. The Kangaroos have shocked the AFL world by parting ways with Alastair Clarkson after four years at the helm. Club president Sonja Hood and football boss Todd Viney are expected to address the media from 2pm AEST.

North Melbourne president Sonja Hood said the Kangaroos were in a better position now than when Clarkson took over, but the club wanted more success.

"We asked Alastair to give our club stability and strength and help return us to the top of the AFL ladder," Hood said.

"Four years later, we have created an environment where our staff and players want to be at our club. This is a testament to the culture Alastair has helped create and the belief that he has built in this group.

"Although we have clearly made progress and won more games, we won't shy away from our desire to want more from this talented group.

"We are incredibly grateful to Alastair for the work he's done over the last four years and we wish him all the very best for his next chapter."

Under Clarkson, North won 20 of their 82 AFL matches, including nine this season. Clarkson took over the Kangaroos after the club had collected back-to-back wooden spoons in 2022 and 2021, while also finishing second-last in 2020.

North have not made the finals in a decade, when the club made consecutive preliminary finals in 2014 and 2015 and an elimination final in 2016 under Brad Scott.

The 2026 season was North's best under Clarkson, and most successful since 2019, with the Kangaroos finishing 14th on the ladder with nine wins.

title: Australian economy grows faster than expected, raising rate hike risk
text:
Australia's economy grew 0.4 per cent in the June quarter, slightly beating most economist forecasts and further raising the prospect of an interest rate hike as soon as this month.

The economy grew 2.1 per cent over the past year to June 30, seasonally adjusted, according to the latest Australian Bureau of Statistics National Accounts.

Both numbers were slightly ahead of economist forecasts, which had centred on a quarterly rise of 0.3 per cent and annual economic growth of 1.8 per cent.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers said the numbers provided further evidence of Australia's relative economic outperformance in challenging global circumstances.

"Annual growth in Australia was as strong or stronger than every major advanced economy – equal to the United States and much stronger than the rest," he said in a press release soon after the data came out.

September rate rise risk jumps

However, IFM Investors chief economist Alex Joiner said the National Accounts highlighted the unsustainability of the growth given current economic conditions.

"Productivity remains poor, per capita GDP was flat [and has lagged other advanced economies materially] and unit labour cost growth elevated," Dr Joiner said.

" The economy risks not slowing quickly enough for the RBA to achieve its inflation objectives and as such it should raise rates in either September or November. "

Traders have subsequently pushed up the odds of a September rate hike by the Reserve Bank of Australia to about 70 per cent, according to Bloomberg analysis of futures market pricing.

The odds of a rate hike at the RBA meeting on September 28-29 were sitting about 50 per cent ahead of today's data.

A rate hike by November is fully priced in, with traders betting on a 20 per cent chance of hikes in both September and November.

Market pricing suggests the RBA's cash rate will peak at 4.8 per cent by the middle of next year, almost two rate rises higher than the current level of 4.35 per cent.

Indeed Asia-Pacific economist Callam Pickering said Australia's labour productivity, defined as real GDP per hour worked, was unchanged in the June quarter, 0.2 per cent lower than a year ago, and 5 per cent below its peak.

"Australian workers today are no more productive than they were seven years ago," he said.

"It turns out artificial intelligence is everywhere, except in the productivity data. We might all be using it, forcing it into our workflows, but it has contributed diddly squat to nationwide productivity.

"We aren't any more productive than we were before these AI tools existed."

However, while he expected another rate rise, Marcel Thieliant from Capital Economics said it was not certain, given growing areas of weakness in key parts of the economy.

"With GDP growth and inflation holding up better than the RBA had anticipated, the bank will probably hike rates again before long, perhaps as soon as this month," he noted.

"A rate hike isn't a done deal yet. After all, the labour market is now clearly loosening and revised data show that the housing downturn has accelerated."

Housing investment and EV boom drive GDP growth

Despite the house price downturn, Mr Chalmers said the National Accounts showed that increased dwelling approvals over the past 18 months were translating into more residential construction.

"A heartening part of today's figures was dwelling investment growth which picked up and broadened in the quarter," he said.

"There were contributions from both new building investment and renovation activity.

"Dwelling investment grew 1.6 per cent in the quarter to be 5.8 per cent higher through the year. This is up from 1.5 per cent in the previous quarter and 4.2 per cent in annual terms."

Household consumption grew 0.4 per cent in the quarter and contributed about half of Australia's overall economic growth during the three months to June 30.

Discretionary spending was the driver, but the ABS said nearly half of the 1.4 per cent jump in the category was due to a surge in vehicle purchases.

"There were record sales of electric and hybrid vehicles as more households looked to lower ongoing operating vehicle costs," the ABS noted in its report.

"The remaining discretionary categories saw subdued growth, where rising cost of living pressures aligned with restrained spending. Domestic and international tourism was particularly weak as the conflict in the Middle East affected travel to the northern hemisphere."

Essentials spending fell 0.3 per cent as a mild winter saw households cut back on heating and high fuel prices saw them reduce the amount of driving they did.

Mr Chalmers said the surge in electric vehicle sales papered over what was generally a subdued outcome for household spending.

"Purchase of vehicles was up 10.3 per cent in the quarter and accounted for almost two-thirds of the quarterly increase in consumption," he said.

title: Live: 'I wasn't happy': Depth of Hadley and Jones animosity revealed in court
text:
Retired 2GB radio host Ray Hadley has begin facing cross-examination at Alan Jones's indecent assault and sexual touching trial.

Veteran broadcaster Alan Jones has pleaded not guilty to 22 charges related to the alleged offending, with the trial in the NSW Local Court now in its fourth week.

Live Moment Live updates, reactions and contributions from ABC readers. Proceedings resume Everyone is now back in the courtroom, with Gabrielle Bashir SC to continue her cross-examination of Ray Hadley. Court breaks for lunch Judge Glenn Walsh has adjourned for the midday break, with proceedings to resume at 2pm. 'I wasn't happy with him' Mr Hadley has been shown a text message he said to Complainant C in October 2019 in which the retired radio host called Mr Jones a homophobic slur. Ms Bashir put to Mr Hadley that he "harboured animosity towards Mr Jones at that time". "I wasn't happy with him," Mr Hadley said in response. The trial heard Mr Hadley had been subpoenaed to produce a number of his own text messages, but that he had not done so. 'Tumultuous relationship' Mr Hadley was next taken to a text message exchange he had with Mr Jones when the latter was unwell in mid-2019. "Mate, sorry you're not well. Hope my elixir didn't make you worse," Mr Hadley said to Mr Jones in one message. "You know I love you xxx. Above ground I mean." Ms Bashir put to Mr Hadley that sentiment was "rubbish". Mr Hadley rejected the suggestion. "I didn't want him to die, obviously," he said. "We had a tumultuous relationship … but I didn't wish him to be ill in health." Meeting with ex-Nine head Hugh Marks examined Ms Bashir has returned to Mr Hadley's "secret" contract to replace Mr Jones as breakfast show host. Mr Hadley said he met with then-CEO of Nine Entertainment, and now managing director of the ABC, Hugh Marks in late 2018 to discuss the contract. Mr Hadley said Mr Marks had no objections to him taking on the breakfast slot. Mr Bashir put to Mr Hadley that he met with Mr Marks with the intention of seeing if he would support Mr Hadley in the role "despite the allegations being made against [Mr Hadley]". Mr Hadley rejected the suggestion. Hadley 'likely' insulted Jones to his face, court hears Mr Hadley tells the court it's "quite likely" he called Mr Jones derogatory names to his face. Ms Bashir has continued to question Mr Hadley about the supposed animosity between himself and Mr Jones. Asked whether he told Mr Jones he was a "c*** and a dog", Mr Hadley replied, "yes, it's quite likely I said that." "I was talking to him about his work," he said. Questioned about whether Mr Hadley was being honest while giving his evidence, the former radio host replied, "I've come here to tell the truth, I'm under oath". Staff told to 'dig up dirt on Hadley', trial hears Mr Hadley said a 2GB colleague, who he described as a "double agent" told him Mr Jones requested that his staff "dig up dirt on Hadley". Defence barrister Gabrielle Bashir SC asked Mr Hadley whether he recalled being accused of assaulting a colleague in the 2GB corridors, which Mr Hadley said CCTV proved never took place. "Fortunately, there was CCTV in corridors and I didn’t come close [to that person]," he said. Mr Hadley told the court he later asked management whether the person who made the accusation would be "disciplined" for making a false complaint. Mr Hadley said he was informed of the accusation by a colleague, who he said was working as a "double agent" for Mr Jones. Hadley took interest in media coverage Mr Hadley has admitted to following the media coverage of Mr Jones's indecent assault trial. He told the court he'd "become more interested in the last few days" but accepted that he had paid some attention to articles written about the hearing throughout the course of the trial. "I didn’t take much notice until I heard from [Jason] Morrison and [another former 2GB colleague]," he said. Shareholder 'had enough of Jones', trial told Mr Hadley said John Singleton, a shareholder of Macquire Media at the time, approached him with the idea of taking over the breakfast slot, saying he'd "had enough of Jones costing him millions" with defamation cases. "I didn’t pursue it, they came to me," he said. The trial heard Mr Hadley was due to take the role in mid-2019 but it never eventuated, and Mr Jones was re-signed for two more years. Mr Hadley rejected multiple suggestions that he was "telling everyone" at 2GB that the breakfast slot was his after he signed the contact. He also denied telling Complainant C about the contract. Details of 'secret' contract revealed Ray Hadley tells the court he signed a contract to replace Alan Jones as the breakfast radio host at 2GB in mid-2019, but only because it would have doubled his salary to $4 million. Mr Hadley said he was approached by management to take the breakfast program and later signed a "secret" contract in late-2018. "They doubled my salary and gave me breakfast money," he said. "I didn’t want to get out of bed at half past one [in the morning] but the money made me do it. "I'll do midnight to dawn for $4 million a year if you want me to." Show more

The court has previously heard a former colleague of Mr Jones, known as Complainant C, has accused the now-85-year-old of kissing him in a work lift on multiple occasions in 2008.

Complainant C also alleges Mr Jones touched his crotch on a number of occasions.

Mr Jones has been taking notes while Mr Hadley gives evidence. (ABC News: Abubakr Sajid)

The trial was previously told Complainant C confided in Mr Hadley in October 2019.

Mr Jones could be seen staring down Mr Hadley as he returned to the witness box for cross-examination for a second day following a brief legal argument on Wednesday.

Mr Hadley accepted a suggestion by defence barrister Gabrielle Bashir SC that he had a "close relationship" with Complainant C before the alleged victim came in regular contact with Mr Jones.

Questions turned to Mr Hadley's relationship with Mr Jones, with Mr Hadley telling the court he "quite likely" called his counterpart derogatory names to his face.

He accepted a suggestion that he likely called Mr Jones a "c*** and a dog".

"I was talking to him about his work," Mr Hadley said.

Ms Bashir also asked Mr Hadley if he recalled being accused of assaulting a colleague in the 2GB corridors.

"Mr Hadley said CCTV video showed the incident never took place.

"Fortunately, there was CCTV in corridors and I didn't come close [to that person]," he said.

Mr Hadley said he was informed of the accusation by a colleague, who he said was working as a "double agent" for Mr Jones.

Ms Bashir pressed Mr Hadley about how honest he had been while giving evidence.

"I've come here to tell the truth, I'm under oath," Mr Hadley said in response.

Conversation with alleged victim probed

Mr Hadley on Tuesday told the trial he consoled Complainant C when he "broke down" while discussing Mr Jones's alleged offending.

The former 2GB star first met Mr Jones in the early 1980s, with the trial on Tuesday hearing evidence about an alleged plot for Mr Hadley to take over his counterpart's coveted breakfast slot in 2019.

Mr Hadley's evidence was cut short on Tuesday afternoon to allow legal arguments to be resolved.

Mr Hadley on Tuesday said he asked Complainant C if he had consented to the kissing and touching.

"[Complainant C] broke down and cried. He said, 'No I hated it. I'm not homosexual'," he said.

"[Complainant C said] he felt a sense of guilt that he allowed it to happen and he wished he'd done something about it."

Mr Hadley says Complainant C became emotional during the conversation about Mr Jones. (ABC News: Abubakr Sajid)

Mr Hadley said the man swore him to secrecy, and rejected offers to report the allegations to police, Mr Jones's management or the chair of the radio station.

"[Complainant C said] 'It would ruin me, it would ruin my career … he's too powerful'," he said.

Mr Hadley said the matter was not raised again by either of the men.

The court heard Complainant C later decided to share his allegations with Sydney Morning Herald (SMH) reporter Kate McClymont, who published an article about the claims in December 2023.

Mr Hadley said he acknowledged the reporting in a pre-recorded radio broadcast, and made a statement to police in June 2024.

The trial continues.

title: Ferrari's Schumacher-inspired livery, F1 leader to cop penalty in Italy
text:
Ferrari will be celebrating the legacy of Michael Schumacher this weekend at its home race, with a special livery dedicated to the seven-time Formula 1 world champion.

This year marks 30 years since Schumacher joined the Scuderia, and 20 years since his final F1 victory in the 2006 Chinese Grand Prix.

Piastri searching for answers as teammate re-enters F1 title picture Oscar Piastri's "disappointing" end to the Dutch Grand Prix leaves the Australian and his McLaren team searching for answers, while his teammate has roared back into the Formula 1 title picture.

With Schumacher at the wheel, Ferrari rose to the top of F1 after years spent without championships.

Ferrari's constructors' championship win in 1999 ended a 16-year wait in the teams' competition, while Schumacher's drivers' championship triumph in 2000 made him the first Ferrari race to become world champion since Jody Scheckter in 1979.

Schumacher won five of his seven drivers' championships with Ferrari, from 2000-2004.

This weekend at the Italian Grand Prix in Monza, a race Schumacher won five times with Ferrari, the Scuderia has a one-off livery which pays tribute to the F1 champion.

Among the features are seven stars on the nose of the car, representing Schumacher's world titles, and drivers Lewis Hamilton — the sport's other seven-time world champion — and Charles Leclerc will wear racing suits that also feature the seven stars and Schumacher's logo.

F1 championship leader to take grid penalty at Monza

Kimi Antonelli has celebrated his 20th birthday as the Formula 1 drivers' championship leader, and heads into his home grand prix with a significant 59-point advantage over his two nearest rivals.

F1 drivers' championship leader Kimi Antonelli is set to start the Italian Grand Prix from the back of the grid. (Reiters: Benoit Tessier)

But the youngest-ever leader of the F1 championship heads into this weekend's race at Monza knowing he has work to do to be near the front of the grid.

Mercedes announced during the previous race weekend in the Netherlands that Antonelli will take an engine penalty this weekend.

F1 teams have an allocation of power unit components they can use in a season. When a driver is fitted with a power unit component that exceeds the allocation, they are handed a penalty at the first event that new part is used.

Mercedes has had multiple power unit issues this year, with Antonelli failing to finish in Barcelona and teammate George Russell suffering issues in Canada and Belgium.

Despite the Italian Grand Prix being Antonelli's home race, Mercedes boss Toto Wolff said now was the right time to do it for the championship leader.

"Our calculations say that that's the best track to take it," Wolff said.

"Obviously, algorithms don't take their nationality into consideration. We're here to fight for a championship and not get the most PR. So yeah, that's what we're going to do."

Monza, known as the Temple of Speed, is expected to be a strong track for Mercedes, which is likely why it is taking the penalty now.

With long straights, there should be plenty of opportunities for Antonelli to pass with his impressive Mercedes power unit.

Monza has been the scene of impressive drives through the field in recent years.

Pierre Gasly won from 10th on the grid driving for AlphaTauri (now Racing Bulls). Max Verstappen won in 2022 after taking a five-place grid penalty, while Lewis Hamilton charged from the last row on the grid to place fifth.

Last year, Isack Hadjar started in the pit lane for Racing Bulls and was able to finish 10th.

ABC Sport will have a live blog of the Formula 1 Italian Grand Prix from 9pm AEST on Sunday, September 6.

title: Meet the emerging artists featured in Primavera 2026
text:
Who decides what is remembered? What happens to the objects and stories consigned to history's rubbish bin? Can we ever truly understand or recapture the past?

These are some of the questions the artists showcased in this year's Primavera exhibition, which features Australian artists aged 35 or younger, are wrestling with.

Exhibition curator Antares Wells travelled to dozens of studios and galleries in every state and territory to find the most compelling emerging artists, finding many were interested in working with archives, or records of the past.

"When you visit that many artists, five different exhibitions could come out of that," she tells ABC Arts.

"But I identified a preoccupation with what I've called traces; an interest in the relics of the past, picking them up and making something new with them.

"I think it's an eternal theme, but what [the artists in Primavera] are doing with it is distinctive."

Now in it's 34th year, dozens of Australian artists have been highlighted by Primavera. (Supplied: Jessica Maurer)

The eight artists featured this year in Primavera approach the theme from different angles, but there's a through-line of the idea of value; why we discard or overlook things.

Wells says it's an exhibition for the head and the heart.

"It's not a cold, big, bad archive — there's a human heart beating in all of these works, even the ones that seem very sleek and detached," she says.

"I hope [visitors] take away a sense of the intellectual and aesthetic vitality of work in this country, the sheer range and diversity of that work, but also the richness of human stories around us."

Murder at sea and suppressed queer history

Callum McGrath's work, History Piece, examines a queer love triangle which ended in the stabbing murder of 19-year-old stoker John "Jack" Joseph Riley on naval ship HMAS Australia II in 1942. The incident sparked complex and often opaque legal proceedings.

The Naarm/Melbourne based artist has often explored queer history in his work, though this thread of the story was initially suppressed by the authorities dealing with the murder.

"The homosexual element really comes out of a confession that the victim made to the surgeon while he was being treated for stab wounds before he died," McGrath says.

"That [confession] letter was left out of the court proceedings, so that bit was a bit difficult, but I found a copy of it in the archives eventually," McGrath says.

"The fact that the letter was left out of the court hearings on the boat, I think, speaks volumes."

Callum McGrath's History Piece delves into a love story with a grisly ending. (Supplied: Callum McGrath)

McGrath recasts the story as a complex intersection of queer history, power and politics. His multimedia often uses overlapping layers of images and text to produce a work that resists easy interpretation.

"It's accumulative and exhaustive," McGrath says of History Piece.

"Rather than having something concise, the idea was to present the evidence as this accumulation of stuff."

McGrath's magpie approach includes a series of line drawings he did of the key people involved in the case. He created images from original photos using digital software, etched them onto glass with a computer-driven cutting tool and in-filled the etching marks with ink.

McGrath says he liked the allusive properties of creating portraits on glass.

"In my mind, glass is a visual storage device. The [portraits] are meant to be physical objects of history containing data and information. It's a way of engraving history on these objects that could be reused."

Weaving history and family connection together

In Linda Sok's Deities in Temples XXI, a sacred art form almost extinguished by the Khmer Rouge regime is both revived and reinvented.

When the regime seized power in 1975, they set about destroying religious or pre-revolutionary artefacts, including pidans, a traditional form of Cambodian silk weaving that people usually hung from the ceiling of a temple.

Linda Sok delves into her family history via screen printing. (Supplied: Eloise Cato)

Often, the only record of the lost pidans was archival cards stored in the National Museum of Cambodia.

Sok, now based in the USA, found re-creating these lost treasures helped her reconnect her with her family and Cambodian heritage. She shared the archival card descriptions with her family, who then drew what they thought each lost pidan looked like.

"I'd moved to the US and was feeling far away from them," she says.

"I had to overcome their hesitancy, but when they began doing the drawings and sketches, they became more open to it."

Rather than using the intricate traditional weaving technique, which can take years to learn, let alone master, Sok devised her own method.

She would pull a group of threads tight, screen-print the images her family had created onto the threads, and then add painted elements.

"Screen-printing was my way of paying homage to the practice without actually replicating it, and putting my own spin on it as well," she says.

Re-creating the pidans led Sok to reflect on how our record of the past is always fragmented and imperfect.

One of the images her family created featured a tree front and centre despite the official record of that pidan, created by French archivists, not mentioning any trees.

"When I went back to Cambodia, I noticed how prevalent the imagery [of trees] was throughout Buddhist iconography, so it was interesting that [my family] chose to reintroduce it," she says.

"Maybe the archivists had thought the tree wasn't important to include, so it got left out.

"There's no way of telling what exactly the truth of the matter is, but it's an interesting question that I've been thinking about a lot."

Meteorites and 'meteorwrongs'

Sometimes, a member of the public believes they've found a meteorite, an exotic item that has travelled to Earth from outer space.

Then they send the item to their local science museum, only to be told it's just a regular rock or a lump of industrial debris.

These items are sometimes called "meteorwrongs", and they're the focus of Meteorite Enquiries, a gently funny and melancholy work by Boorloo/Perth-based artist Jack Wansbrough.

"They're essentially waste, but there's still all this life and personality in them," Wansbrough says of the objects.

Jack Wansbrough's collection of ‘meteorwrongs’. (Supplied: Jessica Maurer)

Working from an archive cataloguing a museum's correspondence on "meteorwrongs", Wansbrough sought to re-create (or find) substitute objects for each oddity and give these rejected items their moment in the sun.

He then displayed the objects on a low floor bed alongside the archive's yellowing letters and beneath a pair of stained-glass fixtures he made.

Wansbrough spent about six months making and sourcing the objects, combing crystal shops, industrial estates, roadsides and even the car park of a university geology department to find what he was after.

Artist's dazzling terracotta earrings celebrate Indian heritage Monica Rani Rudhar's embellished gold earrings are more than just accessories — they are cultural markers connecting her to family.

"Sometimes, I was looking at photos and a piece I literally found on the ground was almost a perfect match. That was really exciting," Wansbrough says.

"But sometimes, the descriptions are extremely brief, which can make it harder but also easier, in a way. Some letters would just say 'A rock that's been carved', so that gave me an interpretive freedom to carve anything I want."

While the rocks and debris Wansbrough's installation re-creates may not be of scientific interest, each has its own idiosyncratic human story.

"With my work, I'm often pointing away from myself, towards an archive or something external. I find it's an interesting way to work in that you're always looking at this thing in front of you, but also imagining this thing that you can't see."

Primavera 2026: Young Australian Artists runs until September 28 at the Museum of Contemporary Art Australia in Sydney.

title: Bledisloe Cup quadruple-header announced as sevens added to ticket
text:
Australia's sevens teams will share the stage in a scheduling first, with the Wallabies and Wallaroos creating a Bledisloe Cup quadruple-header in Sydney.

The Stadium Australia Test against the All Blacks on October 17 already had a support act secured, with the Wallaroos due to host Scotland for the first time in their WXV Global Series clash.

Kick-off times for Bledisloe Cup in Sydney Wallaroos v Scotland, 12pm

Australian sevens men v Fiji, 2:05pm

Australian sevens women v New Zealand, 2.25pm

Wallabies v New Zealand, 3:45pm All times in AEDT

Now two more fixtures will be added to the ticket, with Australia's world champion sevens women to face rivals New Zealand and the men up against two-time Olympic gold medallists Fiji.

"This is an historic moment for Australian rugby, with all four of our Teams In Gold competing on the same pitch, on the same day, on an unmissable occasion," Rugby Australia chief executive Phil Waugh told AAP.

"The day will showcase the very best of rugby with our elite male and female players across the XVs and Sevens formats taking on famous rivals from around the world in an unprecedented line-up of international rugby.

"We look forward to celebrating this extraordinary occasion with our great Australian rugby community and we thank our friends from New Zealand Rugby, Fiji Rugby Union and Scottish Rugby for helping make this day a reality."

The Wallaroos will begin the action before the men's and women's sevens outfits take the field, followed by the Wallabies, who will complete the four-course menu with a late afternoon kick-off at the venue set to host next year's World Cup final.

AAP

title: Live: ASX falls sharply, oil hits two-month high amid US-Iran strikes
text:
When it comes to GDP and inflation data, some analysts make the point that, since both sets of data are backward-looking, it can be a bit misleading to speak about them in annual terms because growth rates from a year ago don't provide much information about what's happening today.

They say one solution is to take the last six months of data and annualise it, because that gives us a better idea of what's happening right now, and Westpac's economics team has done that with today's GDP data.

For example, the data show that Australia's economy expanded 0.4% in Q2 2026, with annual growth slowing to 2.1%.

But it's a different story when you look at the last six months:

"Despite the slight upside surprise, the economy is losing momentum, with growth running at around 1.5% on a six-month annualised basis over the first half of 2026, down from around 2.8% in the second half of 2025," they say.

Having said that, they say the economy is still running a touch firmer than expected by the RBA at this point in the economic cycle.

And they say unit labour costs ticking higher in the June quarter will likely add to the RBA Monetary Policy Board's unease leading into its September meeting.

title: 'No-one told us anything': NT community without services months after floods
text:
At the end of a dust-laden road on the banks of the Daly River, the remote Indigenous community of Nauiyu bears the scars of disaster.

The entrance road is marred by large potholes eating into speed bumps, while mounds of silt line the outskirts of town.

Potholes can still be seen around Nauiyu / Daly River after the remote NT community flooded earlier this year. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

It has been three months since residents of Nauiyu, also known as Daly River, returned home after back-to-back record floods in February and March forced them to evacuate.

Outside his house at the end of town, life-long Nauiyu resident James Parry can point to the exact step the floodwaters rose to.

"It covered 15 stairs — the whole bottom half of the house," he said.

James Parry says his family were lucky because they could move some of their belongings to the second-floor of their home. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

"The tables were flipped over, the couches were flipped, my bed, my freezer."

He said he was one of the luckier members of the community, as he and his family were able to move some of their belongings upstairs.

"Everybody else lost everything — cars, homes, the lot," he said.

James Parry says so many Nauiyu residents lost everything in the floods. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

Mr Parry said the 2026 floods were the worst he has ever seen and there is mounting frustration that key services in the community were not yet fully online.

"The aged care centre is full of asbestos, and we only have a few old people left," he said.

"Kids are not turning up to school since they got back; the teachers have to go around door-to-door to get these kids to come to school."

James Parry showed the ABC areas still damaged by flooding in Nauiyu / Daly River earlier this year. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

He also said various repair works have not been done well, noting large gaps beneath doors leading to dust travelling inside and glass windows replaced with plastic.

"Some of those council homes had wooden benches, wooden drawers, wooden floors, they were all ripped out," he said.

Of particular concern is the boil water alert still in place for the community.

Ever since their return, residents' drinking water supply has come from pallets of bottled water packages routinely unloaded outside the Nauiyu general store.

"No-one's told us anything," Mr Parry said.

The only access to clean drinking water is from deliveries of pallets of bottled water to the town. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

'It doesn't feel like home'

Nauiyu resident Kieren Karritpul said the damage had fundamentally changed the town.

"This place is not really 100 per cent," he said.

"It doesn't feel like home."

As of the end of August, several residential buildings in the community were still without power, impacting living arrangements and preventing key workers from returning to the community.

Kieren Karritpul is reviewing the damage to the Merrepen Arts Centre and its equipment in Nauiyu / Daly River. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

"My brother and my niece have been staying over at my house because their house still doesn't have power," Mr Karritpul said.

On a shady street in the centre of the community, Merrepen Arts Centre, where Mr Karritpul works, stands dormant among mounds of dirt and damaged art materials.

The centre, which employs more than 40 artists, is one of the buildings that has gone without power since the flood, depriving residents of a source of income and community.

Kieren Karritpul says the art centre's closure has meant tourists have to travel to Darwin to purchase local artists' work. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

"Every now and then I get pulled up at the shop or clinic by people asking when it will open, or when they will get their canvases," he said.

" We have to tell [tourists] to go on the three-hour drive to Darwin if they want to buy things. "

Though empty and without power, Merrepen Arts Centre managers have still been issued a power and water bill covering "fixed daily charges" for the first half of 2026.

Questions raised around flood response

The sorry state of Nauiyu several months on from the floods has prompted questions about plans for remediation.

After the last wet season, the Northern Territory government announced a $100 million flood recovery fund to repair damaged infrastructure and aid with flood mitigation.

Daly River faces massive clean-up bill after record flood Residents of the Northern Territory town of Nauiyu / Daly River have started returning home after spending three months in evacuation centres following extensive flooding.

So far, only $12.5 million of the fund has been spent, with just $500,000 put toward Nauiyu in the form of a plan to relocate the town to higher ground.

Labor MLA Dheran Young, who represents the Daly electorate in the Territory parliament, said it was disappointing the community had been left behind

"The CLP government need to apply for the Commonwealth Disaster Relief Fund to ensure services can get back up and running," he said.

" To date, my understanding is that they haven't applied after the disaster relief fund under these extraordinary circumstances. "

In August, the Commonwealth made a million-dollar investment in Nauiyu through the National Indigenous Australians Agency.

"The scale of damage experienced by the community has been immense," Indigenous Australians Minister Malarndirri McCarthy said.

Malarndirri McCarthy says the damage done to Nauiyu from flooding earlier this year has been significant. (ABC: Matt Roberts)

"These investments will support community-led recovery efforts, helping to restore critical community facilities [and] strengthen local services."

The funding package, primarily aimed at local Indigenous corporations, sought to restore essential services, assets and accommodation for key workers.

The Northern Territory government did not respond to questions on Nauiyu or the recovery.

Mr Parry said the community has been visited by engineers and other personnel planning the town's relocation, in accordance with the NT government's investment.

He was frustrated, however, that there has not been more action ahead of the coming wet season.

James Parry says he is frustrated that the NT government has not done more to prepare for the next wet season. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

"You got mango flowering now, you got tamarind, you got the cashew; those three things tell you that the rain's on the way here," he said.

With the near future uncertain, he wants a solid commitment from governments that funding will flow through to key services, and a plan will be in place should flooding re-occur.

"They've got everything, they've got homes to go to," he said.

title: Thea Frodin, Serena Williams's body double in movie, makes US Open debut
text:
Making a US Open debut as a teenager is a daunting task, but American Thea Frodin is no stranger to the bright lights.

The 17-year-old played at her home slam for the first time, going down in straight sets to world number two Elena Rybakina 6-3, 6-2.

There were plenty of fans at Grandstand who were there to see Rybakina, this year's Australian Open champion, but Frodin was a mini-celebrity in her own right.

Frodin, from California, was a body double at the age of 12 in the 2021 film King Richard, a movie starring Will Smith about the rise of Serena and Venus Williams with the help of their father, Richard Williams.

Fordin was the body double for actor Demi Singleton, who played Serena in the film, and is now forging her own path at Flushing Meadows.

There was no Hollywood screenwriting for Fordin's debut, with Rybakina never troubled in the win that came after a near three-hour rain delay.

Fordin was not disgraced in the straight-sets defeat. Down 1-5 in the second set, the teenager fired four aces, saving three match points, to extend the match just one extra game.

"She played really well today, and she has great shots," Rybakina said of her teenage opponent.

Fifth seed comes from behind to avoid another US Open boilover

Italian fifth seed Flavio Cobolli has rallied from two sets down to win his first-round match at the US Open, avoiding another early upset on the men's side.

Flavio Cobolli needed more than four hours, and five sets, to make it to the US Open second round. (Getty Images: Julian Finney)

The French Open runner-up beat Francisco Comesana 3-6, 2-6, 6-3, 6-4, 6-4, finishing his match that lasted 4 hours, 12 minutes, not long after some sun had broken through the clouds and allowed play to start on all the outside courts after a morning of rain.

Cobolli made his first career two-set comeback to avoid joining Novak Djokovic (fourth seed) and Arthur Fils (10th seed) among early losers in a men's draw that was already missing top-ranked Jannik Sinner due to injury.

Cobolli said he took a bathroom break after the second set and decided to change everything.

"So I changed all the dress that I started with today and it works," Cobolli said.

"In grand slams it's never done. You have to fight until the last point."

Ninth seed Taylor Fritz, the 2024 runner-up, rolled to a 6-3, 6-2, 6-4 victory over 18-year-old fellow American Darwin Blanch.

Kokkinakis withdraws from US Open before hitting a ball Thanasi Kokkinakis concedes he may have contested his last US Open without even hitting a ball after the cursed star's body failed him once again.

Madison Keys was the only other player to move into the second round early in a tournament where rain threatened to hamper the schedule for a couple of days.

Showers that began Monday night, local time, and could be on and off through the middle of the week delayed play on all the outer courts, allowing action only in Arthur Ashe Stadium and Louis Armstrong Stadium, which have retractable roofs.

Keys, the 22nd seed, beat 19-year-old Alina Korneeva 7-5, 6-4 in the leadoff match in Ashe. The 2017 US Open runner-up was knocked off in the first round last year in Flushing Meadows.

"It's always tough playing someone young and up-and-coming, and they're going after their shots," Keys said.

"And it's so hard to play a first round of a Grand Slam, so nervous and just wanting to do so well. So, really happy I was able to kind of fight through that and win today."

Coco Gauff, the 2023 US Open champion, 17th seed Alex Eala, and men's first seed Alexander Zverev are scheduled to play later on the final night of round one matches.

It was an action-packed morning at Alan Jones’ criminal trial in the Downing Centre Local Court in Sydney.

If you’re just joining us now, Jones’ long-time talkback colleague at 2GB, Ray Hadley, returned to the witness box today after a brief stint on Tuesday.

Ray Hadley arrives at court on Wednesday. Dominic Lorrimer

Hadley has given evidence that complainant “C”, one of six men who has accused Jones of unwanted touching and kissing, confided in him in late 2019 about the alleged indecent assaults. Jones denies the allegations.

Hadley is now being cross-examined by Jones’ barrister Gabrielle Bashir, SC. She is expected to put to him that he encouraged “C” to make the allegations about Jones because the two broadcasters were professional rivals, but she has yet to launch this line of questioning.

Hadley revealed during his cross-examination that he signed a “secret contract” in late 2018 to take over Jones’ breakfast radio slot at 2GB from July 2019, after he was approached by John Singleton.

Singleton was then a major shareholder in Macquarie Media, the company that owned 2GB.

He said the deal fell over when Singleton sold down his stake in Macquarie Media to Nine Entertainment, the owner of this masthead, but that he insisted 2GB honour the agreement to double his salary from $2 million to $4 million.

Nine has since sold its radio division, and Hadley retired from the airwaves in 2024.

Hadley denied that he regarded the breakfast slot as the pinnacle of professional achievement and said he was motivated by money when he signed the deal.

He denied that it was a difficult time for him when Jones re-signed his contract for two years in May 2019, saying: “Inadvertently Mr Jones had doubled my salary for doing the same job.”

Hadley told the court that a 2GB employee told him in about 2019 that Alan Jones had “marshalled the troops and said, ‘dig up some dirt on Hadley’.” Bashir asked if he had come to court to discredit that 2GB employee. “Not at all, I’ve come here to tell the truth, I’m under oath,” Hadley responded.

Hadley has agreed that he called Jones many derogatory names over the years, and said they had a “tumultuous relationship”. He was taken to a text exchange he had with Jones in 2019 when Jones was sick. Jones had said he had been “crook as Rookwood”, in a reference to the Sydney cemetery. Hadley had joked in response that he loved Jones “above ground”.

The hearing will resume after the lunch break, at 2pm.

North Melbourne have sacked coach Alastair Clarkson after four seasons and with a year remaining on his contract. Players and staff were called into the club for an emergency meeting on Wednesday morning, weeks after the end of their men’s season. Loading Two people with knowledge of the meeting, who spoke on condition of anonymity, confirmed that it was about Clarkson’s future, and members of a coterie group were informed by the club that the 58-year-old would not coach the Roos in 2027. Clarkson was told of the club’s decision on Tuesday after a post-season consultation period during which North bosses sought the views of the football department and players, two sources confirmed.

Advertisement

The leadership’s view, as communicated to the coterie, was that the Kangaroos had made progress under Clarkson but felt they needed to extract more from a talented group. Clarkson issued a statement via his management. Alastair Clarkson is leaving North Melbourne. Getty Images “My time as coach of the North Melbourne Football Club has come to an end,” he said. “We set out to stabilise the club and lay the foundations for a return to playing deep in September.

Advertisement

“The challenge was a difficult one that I embraced with my whole being. “My family and I have been privileged to be involved in AFL football for over 40 years, but it is now time for a new chapter.” Clarkson, who coached Hawthorn to four premierships before departing at the end of the 2020 season, has been with the Kangaroos since his appointment in late 2022. The Roos finished 14th this year with nine wins and 14 losses. They had been in the top 10 with eight wins on June 21 but slumped out of finals contention since.

It was their highest result under Clarkson after finishes of 17th in his first two years in charge and 16th in 2025. “We asked Alastair to give our club stability and strength and help return us to the top of the AFL ladder,” club president Sonja Hood said. “Four years later, we have created an environment where our staff and players want to be at our club. This is a testament to the culture Alastair has helped create and the belief that he has built in this group. “Although we have clearly made progress and won more games, we won’t shy away from our desire to want more from this talented group.

Advertisement

“We are incredibly grateful to Alastair for the work he’s done over the last four years and we wish him all the very best for his next chapter.” Related Article AFL 2026 ‘This is on me, not the club’: Alastair Clarkson opens up on the Roos’ plight Viney, Clarkson’s longtime lieutenant and friend, will remain at the club and is expected to be part of the coach search process. North Melbourne players were spotted emerging from the Roos’ facilities at Arden Street after the meeting but would not comment beyond expressing excitement for next season. As previously reported by this masthead, Clarkson signed a five-year deal worth more than $5 million when he agreed to return to his former club and has a contract that essentially guarantees him the full amount of his 2027 contract, according to sources with knowledge of the deal.

Advertisement

North Melbourne, who have received the highest amount of variable funding from the AFL of Victorian clubs over the past two years (surpassing St Kilda who had long held that mantle), have been a relatively frugal club since the 2000s. The Roos wiped off their debt and enjoyed repeated financial benefits from their stint of playing home games in Hobart and now Western Australia. External discussion of Clarkson’s position and future has included the fact that Adam Simpson and John Longmire – both Kangaroos playing greats who went on to coach AFL premierships at other clubs – are not presently employed as senior coaches. Other potential targets could include Corey Enright and Jaymie Graham, who were contenders for the Carlton and Essendon jobs, respectively, before Josh Fraser and Mark McVeigh were appointed by those clubs. Loading In March, Clarkson told this masthead he was all for someone else taking the top job at North Melbourne if they were better placed for a quicker return to premiership contention.

Advertisement

“I came back here to help the footy club. [It’s] nothing to do with ego, nothing to do with anything else except repay to North what they gave to me as a young fellow,” he said. North had not guaranteed Clarkson’s position when pressed on whether he would coach in 2027 as contracted. Western Bulldogs coach Luke Beveridge was shocked when he was told of Clarkson’s fate midway through his press conference on Wednesday. “Really?” Beveridge said. “Jeez.” Beveridge served as an assistant coach under Clarkson at Hawthorn in 2012-14 when the Hawks won two flags and were narrowly beaten by Sydney in a grand final.

Coles and Woolworths have stopped selling nutritional supplements made from krill, a tiny crustacean that is the major food source for iconic Antarctic wildlife such as Emperor penguins and whales. The supermarket giants confirmed the decision in response to questions from this masthead but both declined to comment further. Krill supplements, taken as a source of Omega-3 fatty acids, are still sold in smaller retailers and most pharmacies. A humpback whale fluking in front of a krill super trawler last summer. Sea Shepherd The withdrawal by Coles and Woolworths comes amid an international campaign by environmental groups to try to curb the burgeoning krill fishing industry because of fears about the pressure on the Antarctic ecosystem. Captain Peter Hammarstedt, director of campaigns at Sea Shepherd Global, drew attention to the Coles move with a LinkedIn post, noting that international retailers UK-based Holland & Barrett and German retailers dm-drogerie markt and Dirk Rossmann GmbH had also withdrawn from the market.

Advertisement

Antarctic krill is the keystone species of the Southern Ocean. Brett Wilks / AAPP “We have already seen market forces begin to shift decisively away from krill in the United Kingdom and Germany,” Hammarstedt said. “Now that change has reached Australian shores.” Holland & Barrett, a health food chain with more than 1000 stores in Britain, helped cofound the Antarctic Krill Pledge, which has since been signed by a number of smaller retailers. Krill-based nutritional supplements are currently worth an estimated $US110.1 million ($154.01 million) globally, according to Future Market Insights, and this is expected to grow to $US216.59 million by 2036, driven largely by demand in China and North America.

Advertisement

The sustainability claims on a bottle of red krill supplements. Audrey Richardson In Australia, krill oil is the fastest-growing source segment within Australia’s Omega-3 supplements market, Complementary Medicines Australia said. Sea Shepherd Global has spent the past few Antarctic summers documenting the krill fishing in Antarctica to raise public awareness, and supporting scientists to study the ecological effects but without trying to prevent operations since krill fishing is a legal activity under international agreements. Captain Paul Watson Foundation took a different approach and engaged in direct action to try to disrupt the krill harvest as much as possible. The rapid increase in the size of the krill fishing fleet over the past few years meant that last month the krill fishery closed early for the second year in a row. The fishery reached its catch limit of 620,000 tonnes and automatically closed on August 12, months ahead of schedule. Emperor penguins rely on sea ice for breeding and as a source of krill. title: Revealed: The failures behind Telstra's major network outage
text:
In brief An independent investigation has found Telstra failed to prioritise systems that led to a major outage.

A separate ACMA investigation, that could result in fines of up to $30 million, is ongoing.

Telstra did not prioritise systems that caused a major nationwide network failure and lacked the technical expertise to properly maintain them, an independent investigation has found.

The results of the review into the telco's 8 July network failure, which left thousands of Australians unable to make calls or access data, were released on Tuesday.

The outage sparked chaos with Triple Zero calls and businesses affected, along with failures across train networks and electronic payment services.

A lack of ownership and oversight of the functions that led to the outage were identified as key contributing factors by Technology Audit Partners in the report.

The outage began at 2.50am, nearly an hour earlier than identified by Telstra at the time.

Following the outage, Telstra confirmed it had conducted welfare checks on those who tried to place more than 600 unsuccessful emergency calls.

The investigation also found a further eight Triple Zero calls did not go through to emergency services during the outage. Welfare checks were conducted in relation to those unsuccessful calls, with no adverse outcomes identified, according to the company.

The outage was triggered by a software update not being done on a GPS card, which resulted in incorrect date information.

It was primarily a result of Telstra not treating network timing as a critical capability, the report found.

On the night of the outage, the two primary engineers involved in the botched upgrade were on mandatory stand-down, the report found.

"The overarching finding is we did not prioritise our timing system inside our networks at the highest level as a critical capability, which is exactly what it should have been," chief executive Vicki Brady told media on Wednesday.

"That is a miss on our side."

Brady said additional resources and expertise had been allocated to the impacted area.

Since the outage, just over 30,000 customers have contacted the telco, which has processed credits of just under $1 million for those customers.

Any customers who felt they were impacted and had not been in contact were encouraged to reach out to the company.

Brady was among 10 senior executives whose bonus was cut as a result of the outage. Her total compensation was $6.8 million, 11 per cent more than the previous year.

"I fully accept the board's decision on that," Brady said.

A separate ongoing Australian Communications and Media Authority investigation into the outage could result in fines of up to $30 million.

title: Four more Australians found safe after Nepal floods as death toll passes 1,000
text:
In brief Four more Australians have been confirmed safe following devastating flooding in Nepal.

It follows news that officials had contacted an Australian in Tibet.

Four more Australians have been confirmed safe in the Nepal-Tibet region following devastating flooding.

Six Australians have now been located since the floods hit the Nepal-China border last Wednesday. Officials were in contact with an Australian in Tibet on Tuesday after another Australian, Cara Severino, was found safe in Nepal over the weekend.

According to the ABC, one of the four other Australians located was found in Nepal. The remaining three were found outside of the location where the flooding took place. Their welfare is currently not known.

The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT) has revised the number of Australians still unaccounted for in the region down to 38.

Australian aid supplies aboard a Royal Australian Air Force plane that departed earlier this week were due to arrive in Nepal on Wednesday morning.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Search and rescue efforts continue

The death toll from devastating Himalayan glacial floods crossed the 1,000 mark on Tuesday, as Chinese and Nepali teams searched for survivors including dozens feared trapped in hydropower tunnels.

Nearly 4,500 people are missing after the gigantic wave of freezing water, rocks and debris triggered by a high-altitude glacial collapse roared downstream on Wednesday, wiping out entire settlements and carving a path of destruction across Nepal.

Nepali rescue teams are digging, drilling and blasting through debris in a desperate race against time to free around 100 hydropower workers believed trapped in multiple tunnels.

So far, rescuers have recovered only bodies from tunnels blocked by sludge, and hopes of finding survivors are fading.

Excavators worked into the night on Tuesday, but an army update noted that "a large amount of water started flowing" into a hole they were digging, forcing them to start a new opening.

Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah has called the catastrophe "unimaginable and heartbreaking".

With mortuaries overflowing in Nepal, authorities have begun burying hundreds of unidentified bodies after DNA sampling.

At least 17 bodies have also been pulled from rivers downstream in India.

Police, using a drone to search for survivors, said on Tuesday that they had located 24 corpses inside a single house in Nuwakot district.

Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal said he still hoped some of the thousands missing could be alive.

"Miracles do happen," he told the Agence France-Presse (AFP) news agency in an interview. "At this point, I do not want to completely give up hope."

'Find their bodies'

In the capital Kathmandu, crowds lined up to search for their missing relatives.

Debu Sapkota, a 58-year-old driver, posted photos of his 83-year-old mother-in-law and her granddaughter, alongside dozens of others.

Sapkota said he had little hope they survived after witnesses saw them being carried away by the torrent.

"I am here hoping to find their bodies," he said.

Some, believing they will never find their missing relatives, held symbolic funerals in accordance with Nepali Hindu customs.

"We searched everywhere, went to morgues across the country, but could not find his body," said Jeevan Shrestha, as his 12-year-old nephew set fire to a tiny straw effigy representing his missing father.

Aid needs are enormous. Entire communities have been swept away, leaving families homeless and using makeshift shelters as heavy rain lashes down.

Roads and dozens of bridges have been smashed, and power plants destroyed.

"There are too many challenges," police officer E Hawadi said in the badly affected Nuwakot district.

Climate change

AFP photographers in Nuwakot on Tuesday saw people scouring the mud for usable items and stringing up plastic sheeting for shelter amid the ruins.

Foreigners missing among the list include 583 in Nepal and 261 in China, coming from more than 30 nations.

They include tourists who had come to trek in the Himalayas, as well as Hindu pilgrims seeking spiritual peace at Tibet's sacred Mount Kailash.

Nepal's economy is already under pressure, with limited resources to respond to a disaster of this scale.

Kathmandu has warned reconstruction costs could run into the "billions of dollars".

There is growing anger at the scale of the destruction that has hit Nepal, a largely rural nation of 30 million people.

The country has contributed little to the greenhouse gas emissions driving global warming, but is among those suffering its consequences.

Khanal, the foreign minister, told AFP that the "disaster should be seen as a warning signal to the risk that climate change poses to Nepal", adding that support should be seen "from a perspective of climate justice".

Scientists say the Himalayas, the world's highest mountain range, are warming rapidly as global temperatures rise, accelerating glacier melt.

Glaciers in the wider Himalayan and Hindu Kush ranges are a crucial water source for around 240 million people in the mountainous regions, as well as for another 1.65 billion people in the South Asian and Southeast Asian river valleys below.

"It impacts the entirety of the Himalayan region's civilisation," Khanal said.

'Mourn the victims'

Nepal said 1,050 bodies had been recovered by Tuesday, while 3,916 people remained missing.

China's state media reported 16 dead and 546 missing.

That takes the overall number of reported dead to 1,066 and missing to 4,462.

In China, Tibet is largely inaccessible to foreign journalists, and Chinese authorities are the only source of official information.

More than 2,000 people are aiding rescue operations, including soldiers, Xinhua added.

It said on Tuesday that teams were "working around the clock to search for survivors, repair roads, set up communication base stations and restore power lines".

Tibetan advocacy groups in exile have questioned China's account of the disaster, but Beijing insists that the "release of information has been open, transparent and timely".

They then promote good looks and dominance over women as markers of male worth.

Contos will tell the Press Club men who subscribe to those ideals are twice as likely to binge drink and eight times as likely to have suicidal thoughts as their peers.

They are also 17 times more likely to have hit their partner.

Australian teenage boys aged 16 to 18 are committing sexual assault against children more frequently than adults are, the Australian Child Maltreatment Study found in 2023.

Sexual choking sparks calls for action

The federal government is currently exploring whether Australians should be able to opt out of algorithmically curated social media feeds, Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek told ABC Insider's program on Sunday.

The announcement came after a 16-year-old Sydney girl's death was linked in media reports to a suspected sexual choking act — a behaviour often promoted to teenage boys through pornography and social media content.

Contos will tell the Press Club that, while the change would be positive, harsher crackdowns are needed.

She will suggest feeds should only show posts from people users follow, unless users explicitly opt out, to circumvent harmful content. Such a move would revert social media algorithms to how they were a decade ago.

"(The change) would fundamentally make the transition onto social media for 16-year-olds and other children safer, and it would bring the principle of affirmative consent to our screens," Contos will say.

"It is too easy for big tech to design schemes that appear as structural reform but actually suit them just fine."

Teach Us Consent has been running a campaign promoting the change since 2025.

An open letter to the prime minister requesting an end to algorithmic feeds without an opt-out choice has been signed by more than 13,000 Australians.

title: I've worked with families of missing people for 25 years. Here's how uncertainty feels
text:
The surging death count from the devastating flash floods that hit Nepal and Tibet on 26 August has passed 1,000.

At least 42 Australians are among more than 4,000 people still “unaccounted for”. But this phrase "unaccounted" — frequently used in media reports — can split the problem too simply: people are either lost or yet to be found.

For many families waiting for news, this gap between uncertainty and despair is ambiguous — and it’s agonising. There is no guarantee news will ever come.

So, how can people missing loved ones make sense of this traumatic experience while the search continues? And what kind of support will they need?

I have been working with families of missing people for more than 25 years. Here’s what I’ve learnt about their experiences of ambiguous loss.

What is ambiguous loss?

Ambiguous loss describes an ongoing loss without a resolution or closure. It can affect how people feel and behave, and the kind of support they will need.

While waiting for news of their loved ones in Nepal and Tibet, people will be grappling with the shock and trauma of how the disappearance unfolded, and the scale of the disaster. They will also be facing uncertainty and fear about how long they will be on this path.

When living with an ambiguous loss, it is common to oscillate between hopeful thinking and moments of hopelessness.

People may feel frozen to the time they learned the news, replay their last conversations with that person, or repetitively think up new ways to search and find them.

Families in Australia may also feel helpless being so far away, especially as the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade has asked people to reconsider travelling to the affected areas to look for people who are out of contact. They may feel excluded from searching because they can’t travel to the region.

They may also experience physical and emotional agitation, feel sick in the stomach, or be restless from the need to constantly be on alert for information updates.

Validate both hope and hopelessness

When observing how people respond to a missing loved one, it can seem to others that families aren't embracing reality. This might look like clinging to ideas that someone is alive, against the odds, or hoping for a miracle in unlikely circumstances.

This isn’t a family’s decision to not confront the reality, but a normal response to incomprehensible and traumatic situations.

Social workers who work in the field of missing persons learn to encourage families to respond however they need— even if that changes minute by minute.

For many people, surges of hope sustain us in times of crisis and can be a strategy to survive uncertainty. Families not wanting to discuss the potential for a devastating outcome should not be framed as harboring "false hope", but as implementing a boundary that needs to be respected.

For others, there will be comfort in naming fears and imagining the worst. This allows them to voice the private stories that may be echoing in their minds, as they wait for news. While having someone missing is not a dress rehearsal for the grief that may be ahead, speaking the truth about the potential outcomes of a search, can make people feel less alone.

It’s important for people waiting for news to have safe spaces to discuss what they’re feeling and fearing, without judgement.

These private conversations might differ from public narratives (in the media or amid search efforts) which may focus on staying positive and be strength-based.

How to support families of missing people

Don’t speculate.

As a friend or supporter, it's not your job to tell people how to survive this moment. And speculating about possible outcomes can be cruel and unhelpful. Offering compassion and allowing yourself to be guided by what they say and want to talk about is key.

Don’t tell them to 'switch off'.

It may feel tempting to suggest friends or families turn away from traumatic news coverage. But this idea can feel impossible for those affected.

Instead, you could offer to consume news on their behalf, or take responsibility for answering phones or responding to messages. This may give them a small moment of respite.

READ MORE How Australians can help those impacted by devastating Nepal floods

Encourage them to channel their physical reactions to uncertainty.

People waiting for news, far away from the disaster, may be feeling agitated and constantly on alert. Even a short walk around the block or a few minutes of stretching can help manage the constant rush of adrenaline.

Sensory activities that ground you — such as naming something you can hear, see and feel — can also provide simple moments of certainty.

It’s OK to suggest self-care, but it’s best to do it gently and take their lead on what they might need. Attending to all of those activities that simply keep people functioning daily — sleeping, eating, showering — can also be important reminders.

The bottom line

When people are experiencing ambiguous loss, they need people around them to show compassion and be flexible, as they survive this moment. They may need to focus on just getting through the night, the hour, or even the next five minutes.

If you’re supporting someone waiting for news, take care of yourself too. For support options reach out to the National Missing Persons Coordination Centre, which is part of the Australian Federal Police.

Sarah Wayland is a professor of social work at CQUniversity Australia.

title: The COVID trend Australia wasn't expecting this winter
text:
IN BRIEF COVID-19 cases are down 56 per cent on last year, despite infections beginning to rise again over the past fortnight.

Experts are pointing to population immunity and a more stable virus.

Australia appears to have avoided the winter surge in COVID-19 cases seen in previous years, according to a recent report.

Federal surveillance data shows 64,357 COVID-19 cases have been reported so far this year, 56 per cent fewer than the 146,232 cases recorded over the same period in 2025.

The latest figures paint an unusual picture of Australia's COVID-19 landscape, with infections remaining well below last year's levels even as cases begin to tick upwards across the community.

"In contrast to previous years, national data in 2026 to date do not yet show a clear winter peak," the Australian Centre for Disease Control said in its latest respiratory surveillance report.

Experts says changing virus behaviour and population immunity are possible explanations.

Where has the winter wave gone?

Professor Catherine Bennett, chair of epidemiology at Deakin University, said the absence of a clear winter peak was significant.

She said Australia's experience reflected a population that had gradually developed greater immunity to the virus through previous infections and vaccination.

"When you have variants that stay in circulation for a longer period of time, more people have had their immunity naturally boosted against that variant, and that then keeps infection rates down," she said.

Bennett said having fewer major changes in the variants circulating than earlier in the pandemic may be helping people's existing immunity provide greater protection against severe infection.

Rather than a substantially different variant emerging every few months in Australia, the same dominant variant was continuing to circulate, allowing immunity in the population to remain "primed".

Have COVID-19 patterns changed?

Epidemiologist professor Adrian Esterman told SBS News that the pattern of COVID-19 outbreaks had changed significantly over the past few years.

"We aren't actually seeing waves anymore, or if we do have waves they're very small ones," he said.

Esterman said smaller increases in cases now tended to coincide with the emergence of a variant that was better able to transmit or evade existing immunity.

The experts said that a major change to the virus' genetics could still trigger a larger wave, but said there was currently little evidence of one developing.

"Unless there's a huge genetic shift in the virus ... that's the only thing that could disrupt things and cause another wave," Esterman said.

Fewer cases detected

The sharp fall in reported cases raises the question of whether fewer Australians are getting COVID-19, or if fewer infections are being detected.

Reported COVID-19 cases are only a proportion of all infections, meaning surveillance data cannot capture every person who contracts the virus.

But Bennett said she believed the lack of a winter peak was broadly consistent with what was being seen in other measures of COVID-19 severity.

She pointed to hospitalisation data showing COVID-19 was now causing less severe disease among younger and healthier adults than earlier in the pandemic.

At the same time, she warned that there were still important gaps in Australia's understanding of the virus, particularly in relation to the longer-term consequences of infection.

Why immunity could be making a difference

Bennett said repeated exposure to COVID-19 may now be giving many people protection against severe illness without necessarily preventing them from becoming infected.

People may therefore experience very mild infections that are never detected, or fight off infections without becoming noticeably sick.

Bennett and Esterman told SBS News that if the same variants continue circulating, people who have previously encountered them may have enough immunity to prevent infections from producing the large rise in cases Australia has seen in previous winters.

"It's sort of keeping our immunity levels primed up naturally," Bennet said.

But she said that protection is not evenly distributed.

Bennett said older people and those who are immunocompromised may not develop the same strength of immune response from previous exposure, which is why vaccination remains important for those groups.

What happens as we head into spring?

According to the latest federal surveillance report, COVID-19 cases have started increasing again over the past fortnight.

But neither expert believes the rise signals the start of another major wave.

Bennett said the increase needed to be watched, particularly for evidence of a new variant gaining a foothold.

She said a new variant could potentially produce a summer surge, but there was currently no strong trend suggesting that was happening.

Esterman similarly expects the virus to continue producing relatively small increases in cases rather than the large, distinct waves seen earlier in the pandemic.

Could this become the new normal?

The absence of a winter peak does not mean COVID-19 has disappeared, or that future winters will necessarily look the same.

Both experts said that while Australia's 2026 experience could represent an important shift in the way COVID-19 behaves as an endemic respiratory virus, a significant change in the virus could alter the current pattern.

Bennett said the combination of declining transmission, population immunity and a more stable virus had put Australia in a much stronger position than it was in the early years of the pandemic.

"It's very unusual but an important sign that our population-level immunity is still evolving and maturing and putting us in a much better position to cope with an endemic disease like COVID-19."

And if the current trend continues through the warmer months, she said Australia could be entering its quietest 12-month period of COVID-19 transmission in years.

"If we can get through summer without another wave, then that will be the best 12 months we've had for a long time with COVID-19."

title: What's behind the 'biggest oil deal in world history' Trump is touting with Venezuela?
text:
In Brief Donald Trump says the US has signed an agreement that gives the US a stake in Venezuelan oil reserves.

The deal has been thrown into question by experts who question its legal and economic validity.

Details are emerging about what United States President Donald Trump is calling "the biggest oil deal in world history" with Venezuela.

Trump said the agreement announced on Saturday would give the US a stake in Venezuela's vast oil reserves, a step toward his goal of extracting energy from the country after US forces captured then-president Nicolás Maduro in a middle-of-the-night raid in January and brought him to New York to face federal drug trafficking charges.

Venezuela's acting president, Delcy Rodríguez, described the deal as a step toward economic recovery that will modernise the country’s oil industry.

In a televised address to the nation on Sunday, Rodríguez insisted Venezuela's sovereignty is secure and said she wants the country to become a global energy powerhouse.
