On Tuesday, the White House released a fact sheet about the arrangement.

Here's a look at what's known about the deal — and what remains unclear.

What are the terms?

The US government and a private operator in Venezuela have formed a new company that has been granted rights to access untapped oil fields for 100 years.

A statement from Rodríguez said the deal involves the development of 17 fields with a proven potential of 65 billion barrels.

It said the agreement could draw US$100 billion ($139 billion) in investment into Venezuela's oil industry and yield over US$209 billion ($291 billion) in taxes for the country.

The private operator is North America Blue Energy Partners, owned by Alejandro Betancourt, the White House confirmed on Tuesday.

The company currently produces about 200,000 barrels a day, which makes it the second-largest private operator in Venezuela behind Chevron, according to a source who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to release the information.

Trump said the agreement was negotiated by US secretary of state Marco Rubio, defence secretary Pete Hegseth and Rodríguez.

The deal will give the US a 35 per cent ownership stake in the company, and the US state department will get a guarantee to buy 20 per cent of the output at cost. US purchases of oil will go towards US strategic oil reserves along with the military, according to a US official who was not authorised to discuss the matter publicly and spoke on the condition of anonymity.

The company would be the second largest corporate holder of proven reserves after Saudi Aramco, according to the US official.

Bob McNally, who was an energy adviser in former US president George W Bush's administration, said the current administration appears to be seeking ways to make it easier for the private sector to invest in Venezuela's industry through the deal.

"However, investors will remain cautious even if the terms of the deal, once released, pass legal muster. A future president could withdraw, and Caracas has twice thrown foreign investors out," McNally said.

Amos Hochstein, who was a senior energy adviser to former US president Joe Biden, said the deal is uncharted territory from a legal and diplomatic perspective.

It carries tremendous risk for companies thinking about doing business under the new arrangement, he said. Democrats could challenge the deal if they regain power in the US, as could future administrations in Venezuela.

"There will be a lot of challenges to what was just announced," Hochstein said. "I can only say, if it were me, I'd be nervous. And if I'm back in my old job in the next administration, then they should be nervous."

How have Venezuelans reacted?

Some in Venezuela have considered the deal a betrayal of what their government has stated repeatedly for decades: Venezuelan resources are for Venezuela, and leaders would not allow the US government access to those resources.

Harvard University professor Ricardo Hausmann, a former Venezuelan planning minister, called it a "shameful deal".

"Venezuelans will not respect this illegitimate deal and no major US oil company will take it seriously because they know it will not last,” Hausmann said on social media, adding that Rodríguez "has no legitimacy or constitutional power to commit Venezuela to any such deal".

In her national address, Rodríguez pushed back on some early criticism.

"One thing must be absolutely clear: Venezuela retains ownership and sovereignty over its resources," Rodríguez said.

She said the goal is to reach other agreements with transnational private companies such as Chevron, Repsol and Shell.

What's the reaction in the US?

It is unclear whether US congress will play a role in the arrangement, but politicians from both parties were quick to weigh in. Trump allies called it a win.

Republican senator Bernie Moreno said it was a historic deal that would help both countries.

"If it were up to DC Democrats, Maduro would still be in power, Venezuelan oil would be going to China at half price, and the people of Venezuela would be getting robbed by a corrupt regime," Moreno said in a post on social media.

It was widely condemned by Democrats who said Maduro's capture was a means to this end.

What questions remain?

Many important details remain unclear, including who will cover necessary investments and how America's stake in the company breaks down.

The US will get 55 per cent of the company's effective output, but it was not clear what portion of that comes from an ownership stake and how much comes from the right to buy oil at cost.

It is also unclear how the industry will react. Persuading big US oil companies to return to the region could prove challenging given the political uncertainty and damaged infrastructure.

READ MORE Why Australia ships out its wealth — and buys it back as finished goods

David Oxley, chief climate and commodities economist at Capital Economics, said that on its face, the deal could double US oil reserves and reduce dependence on crude oil from Canada and Mexico.

But Oxley, writing in a commentary, cautioned that there are logistical hurdles and said the value of Venezuela's reserves may have been exaggerated under former Venezuelan president Hugo Chávez.

Even with legal and security guarantees, it is not clear that US oil companies "would be eager to invest", he wrote, noting that "there simply might be more enticing commercial opportunities on offer elsewhere".

title: SBS confirmed as Australia's home of the 2030 FIFA World Cup
text:
IN BRIEF: SBS has secured exclusive rights to broadcast the 2030 World Cup live and free to all Australians.

The agreement strengthens a 40-year relationship between SBS and FIFA.

SBS has cemented its place as Australia’s spiritual home of football, securing exclusive national rights to the FIFA World Cup 2030.

Football-loving Australians will have access to all 104 matches of the 2030 tournament via SBS television, video and radio programming.

SBS managing director Jane Palfreyman said the broadcaster is "without question" Australia’s home of the World Cup.

"The FIFA World Cup is one of the few sporting events that truly brings Australians together across all cultures, languages and communities," she said.

"In 2030 audiences will once again be able to experience every match live and free on SBS."

Celebrating its centenary year, the 2030 FIFA World Cup will be the most geographically diverse tournament in the competition’s history.

It will be the first in history to be played across six host nations — with the opening three matches taking place in Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay before the tournament moves to primary host countries Morocco, Portugal and Spain.

All six host nations will automatically qualify for the tournament.

"Our job is to capture the football, the stories, the cultures and the emotion that make it unlike anything else in world sport. We’re incredibly proud to have the opportunity to do that again in 2030."

title: 'It hurts': Lionel Messi announces international retirement after World Cup final defeat
text:
In brief Lionel Messi has announced his retirement from international football.

His domestic contract with Inter Miami continues until the end of the 2028 season.

Lionel Messi said on Tuesday he was retiring from international football after leading Argentina to a second successive World Cup final in July.

The 39-year-old forward, who won the World Cup in 2022 and dragged his nation to the final in the United States only to lose to Spain, said the decision had been painful.

"It was a decision that hurt and still hurts deep in my soul but I understand that it is the right time," Messi wrote on Instagram.

"I swear I always gave everything, not just in the last few years when we won everything but before that too, and I always fought and gave my all for this shirt," he added.

Messi led Argentina to World Cup glory four years ago by winning the final against France in a penalty shootout in Doha, but his side lost 1-0 to a superior Spain side in the 2026 final in East Rutherford, New Jersey.

Following the death of his father Jorge in August, Messi had said he had "serious doubts" about continuing to play football of any sort for "much longer".

"I don't know what I'll do without you, I don't know how to go on. I just played football, and now I have serious doubts about continuing to do so for much longer," he said then.

Messi's contract with Major League Soccer club Inter Miami runs until the end of the 2028 season.

The highlight of Messi's international career was winning the 2022 World Cup in Qatar. Source: Getty / Jean Catuffe

In this year's finals, Messi inspired Argentina to another final by scoring eight goals and provided two assists in the dramatic late comeback against England in the semi-finals.

But the dream of lifting the trophy again proved one match too far as the South Americans lost to Spain at MetLife Stadium (dubbed New York New Jersey Stadium for the duration of the World Cup).

Messi was pictured in tears after receiving his loser's medal. He said afterwards that the pain of defeat was "immense" and that it would "take a long time for this wound to heal".

'Thank you for everything'

In his statement on Tuesday, the eight-time Ballon d'Or winner said it was time for a new generation of Argentina players to take up the torch.

"I love, I loved, and I will always love being on the national team," he wrote. "I gave everything I had, I have nothing more to give, and besides, there are some very talented young players coming up behind me who deserve to be there."

Reacting to the news, FIFA president Gianni Infantino called Messi "one of the greatest players our sport has ever seen" and thanked him for "bringing so much joy to millions of football fans".

First called up in 2005 by Jose Nestor Pekerman as an 18-year-old, Messi would go on to play 207 times for Argentina and become the country's leading scorer, with 125 goals.

Messi also won two Copa Americas in 2021 and 2024 during his 21-year international career.

Yet, before the trophy-laden later years, Messi did not hold the place in Argentine hearts reserved for other national idols such as Diego Maradona or Pope Francis.

After moving to Catalonia at 13 to join Barcelona, Messi could have represented Spain but chose Argentina.

His long-time team-mate Angel Di Maria, also a 2022 world champion, on Monday paid homage to Messi for this choice and his impact on the national team.

"We will be forever grateful to you for being Argentinian and for having taken Argentina to the top of the world," Di Maria said.

"For having chosen to be Argentinian when you could have chosen something else. Thank you for everything."

For Ernesto Godoy, a 38-year-old teacher in Buenos Aires, Messi's retirement from international football marks "the end of an incredible career, a sportsman of a calibre rarely seen".

"There was Maradona, then a void, then Messi, and now we're going to experience that void (again), life without Messi, just as Argentina did without Maradona," he told the Agence France-Presse news agency, of the player who hangs up his shirt assured of his place in the Argentine pantheon.

title: AusPost boss reveals future of letter deliveries a‌mid stamp price warning
text:
IN BRIEF Australia Post says it will keep home delivery, ruling out community mailboxes for Australian suburbs and towns.

Letter deliveries could become less frequent as Australia Post adapts to falling volumes, Graham says.

Australia Post has warned the cost of sending a letter could eventually rise to $2, as the postal service grapples with a continuing collapse in mail volumes.

Chief executive Paul Graham told SBS News that Australia Post will need to make further changes to the way letters are delivered as fewer Australians use the service, but has ruled out any plans to follow overseas postal services that have moved away from traditional home delivery.

"We continue to see letter decline, 15 per cent last year and we're now seeing letter volumes that we haven't seen since the 1930s," Graham said.

The company has already reduced letter deliveries to every second day and increased the price of a standard stamp, but Graham said further price increases and efficiencies would be needed as letter volumes continued to fall, including potentially reducing delivery frequency even further.

Graham said the company is "in the fight of our lives", as it navigates structural change and fierce parcel competition squeezes margins.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Stamp prices could reach $2

Graham said Australia Post's current $1.85 lowest-cost stamp remained among the cheapest in comparable economies.

He said that the price of a stamp could eventually rise, but argued the increase would have a relatively small impact on individual households.

He estimated a further increase to $2 would add less than a dollar a year to the cost for a typical household.

The changes are being driven by the widening gap between the cost of maintaining a nationwide letter service and the number of letters being sent.

Australia Post delivered 1.42 billion letters last financial year, almost 15 per cent fewer than the previous year.

At the same time, its parcels and services business continued to grow, generating a record $8.01 billion in revenue.

No plans to follow in the footsteps of global services

Despite the pressure on its traditional letter business, Graham said there were no plans for Australia Post to follow postal services overseas by abandoning home delivery or shifting customers towards community mailboxes.

He pointed to the different nature of Australian cities, suburbs and regional communities as a reason.

"The nature of our suburbs and regional towns does not lend itself to that solution," he said.

READ MORE Australia Post to lift US shipping pause — but some customers still face a wait

Instead, Graham said Australia Post wanted to tailor its services to the needs of different communities.

He said the organisation remained "absolutely committed" to ensuring efforts to reduce costs did not come at the expense of people living in regional and remote Australia.

Australia Post currently operates more than 4,000 retail outlets across the country, with about 2,500 in regional and remote areas.

Letters still have a future, though it is changing

Graham acknowledged there was a risk Australia Post could eventually require taxpayer support as its letter business continued to decline.

But he said the organisation had a pathway towards financial sustainability, which would require support from government, stakeholders, customers and the broader community.

The company recorded a pre-tax profit of $31.8 million for the latest financial year, although that result was supported by returns from property sales.

Graham said further changes to the postal service would be necessary as Australians increasingly shift from letters to parcels and digital communication.

He urged Australians to continue using Australia Post and supporting its network of licensees across metropolitan, regional and remote communities.

"We'll continue to deliver letters until the last letter needs to be delivered."

title: Grand Canyon flash flood leaves two dead, 'more than 20' missing
text:
In brief Flash flooding has swept through the Grand Canyon National Park in the US.

More than 60 people have been evacuated from the depths of the canyon.

One body has been recovered following flash flooding in Grand Canyon National Park over the weekend, and recovery operations were underway for a second body on Monday, the National Park Service (NPS) told the Reuters news agency.

Heavy rainfall brought surging waters through the canyon on Sunday, destroying trails and footbridges, damaging infrastructure that carries water for use throughout the park, and forcing 62 hikers to be evacuated by helicopter by Sunday morning, according to the NPS.

Park officials reported on Monday that the body of a 46-year-old man had been found. In a post on X, the NPS said "more than 20 individuals" might be missing or unaccounted for and sought information from the public about any hikers who might have been in the path of the raging waters.

In response to questions from Reuters on Tuesday, the NPS confirmed the existence of the second body but did not offer more details about the victim or provide an updated count of the missing.

With additional thunderstorms expected early this week and stringent water-use restrictions in place, the South Rim of the park remained open during the day on Tuesday but overnight accommodations and other concessions were closed.

title: Why China is censoring footage of the Nepal-Tibet disaster
text:
In brief Videos circulating globally of the Tibet-Nepal flood disaster cannot be found on Chinese social media platforms.

The disaster has cast a spotlight on the tight controls over information from Tibet.

A natural disaster may not seem inherently political. But in Tibet, even footage of a flood can be sensitive.

As videos circulated widely on social media and in news reports last week, showing a devastating torrent of mud, water and debris tearing through a border post between Tibet and Nepal, correspondents in Beijing began to point out a striking absence: in China, the footage was nowhere to be seen.

The apparent censorship highlights the extraordinary sensitivity surrounding Tibet, one of the most tightly controlled regions under Chinese control, and the long and highly contested history stretching back hundreds of years.

Tsering Yangzom, a member of the Tibetan community in Newcastle, NSW, told SBS News her uncle works in the flood-affected region of Tibet, but she's been unable to contact him since the disaster and appears to have been blocked.

She suspects he may be concerned their communications are being monitored, but she's also "really, really worried" about whether he was affected by the deadly floods.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Normally, she says they speak briefly and intermittently on the Chinese messaging app WeChat, sometimes using coded language to protect her uncle.

"If he says the weather is good, then we can talk a little bit more about the normal life," she said. "But if he says the weather is not good and rainy or something ... that means that I can't talk much."

Tsering Yangzom said she communicates with her Tibetan relative in code to keep him safe. Source: Supplied

Human Rights Watch's Australia director, Daniela Gavshon, told SBS News censorship and self-censorship are pervasive in Tibetan areas.

"These information controls make it even harder to get accurate information, for families to locate loved ones, or to develop a good understanding of the disaster, its scale, its impact, and the response."

A brief history of China and Tibet

Tibet, isolated both geographically and diplomatically, sits atop a vast area of mountains and plateaus and is often referred to as the "roof of the world".

For centuries, it has had a complicated relationship with China. Beijing maintains that Tibet has been part of China since ancient times, while Tibetans say it had long been independent with its own unique culture, religion and language.

In 1950, troops from China's newly established communist government invaded Tibet and defeated Tibetan forces, in a move the Chinese government described as part of the "peaceful liberation" of the region.

The following year, Tibetan representatives signed an agreement recognising Chinese sovereignty over Tibet, while promising the region autonomy. Tibetan leaders say they were forced into this agreement.

Tensions over Chinese rule grew in the following years, leading to an uprising in 1959 in the Tibetan capital, Lhasa. Thousands are believed to have died during China's suppression of the uprising, and Tibet's spiritual and then-political leader, the Dalai Lama, fled to India, where he has lived in exile ever since.

In 1965, China formally established the Tibet Autonomous Region, which continues to exist today, though its autonomy is highly disputed.

Human rights groups and the Tibetan government-in-exile continue to accuse Chinese authorities of seeking to erase Tibetan religious practice, language and cultural expression, exercising total political control over the region, repressing dissent and blocking the flow of information in and out of Tibet.

Access to the region is tightly controlled, making reporting from within Tibet extremely difficult.

The BBC's China correspondent, Laura Bicker, said she has often found it easier to contact sources in North Korea than in Lhasa.

Why censor a flood?

According to various international media organisations, videos filmed and uploaded by local residents showing the disaster have been censored on Chinese social media platforms.

On Chinese social media platform RedNote, SBS Chinese was unable to find the widely viewed CCTV footage showing the flash flooding engulfing the Rasuwagadhi border crossing between Tibet and Nepal.

Chinese state media has, however, shown vision of recovery efforts.

"For China, everything is inherently political when it comes to Tibet," Zoë Bedford, executive officer of the Australia Tibet Council, told SBS News.

Source: SBS News

"What they're afraid of is people hearing Tibetan voices. They're afraid of people understanding the extent of China's mega-development in Tibet and how much they have been interfering in the environment."

Feng Chongyi, associate professor in China Studies at the University of Technology Sydney, said many Tibetans and Nepalese people blame the Chinese government, which has funnelled billions into developments in the region in a bid to harness its vast hydropower potential and resources.

"The Chinese government, of course, do not want that kind of opinion or discussion to spread to the international community," he told SBS News.

SBS News has approached the Chinese embassy for comment.

The Tibetan Plateau region, sometimes called the world's "Third Pole", has the world's largest ice mass outside the Arctic and Antarctic.

The Himalayan region is particularly vulnerable to a warming climate, with destabilising glaciers increasing the risk of sudden and catastrophic floods like the ones last week that have killed hundreds of people and left thousands more unaccounted for.

The disaster was triggered by a glacier collapse, which Chinese authorities and international experts have linked to climate change.

Just three months before the disaster, officials from China and Nepal met to discuss strengthening cooperation to monitor floods, weather and glacier-related hazards.

But two Nepali officials told the Reuters news agency they didn't receive as much information as they wanted from China on glacier risks and water levels, heightening fears that insufficient data sharing could make it harder to anticipate and prepare for natural disasters.

On Saturday, the Chinese embassy in Nepal posted a statement on X responding to accusations on Nepali social media that it had failed to warn Nepal of the mudslide disaster.

It said China faced significant challenges in monitoring risks in the vast, remote Himalayan region and had always shared "important information with the Nepali side in a timely manner".

title: Should smart glasses blur your face by default? Australia's tech watchdog thinks so
text:
In brief The Australian eSafety Commissioner has recommended changes to how smart glasses operate.

Further new protections will overhaul Australia's privacy laws related to social media, AI and smart glasses.

People's faces should automatically be blurred when being filmed by smart glasses as part of greater privacy measures, the online safety watchdog has urged.

In advice to industry, the eSafety Commissioner has called for extra protections to be put in place for smart glasses, or glasses with cameras attached to them.

The growing uptake of the technology, prompted by cheap versions of the products being sold in outlets such as Kmart, has increased concerns about privacy and people being filmed without their consent.

The commissioner said faces of people being filmed should be blurred by default if they have not given consent, with clearer indicators being given for when the glasses are recording video.

"Companies selling smart glasses must balance the benefits of the technology with the need to protect users and the public," the commissioner said.

"As smart glasses become more common, they may create new ways to perpetrate harms."

The eSafety Commissioner said the rapid evolution of the technology meant there was still a chance for extra safety features to be baked into the products before harms became more widespread.

"They may become increasingly interconnected with and create new ways to perpetrate different types of harms, such as image-based abuse, adult cyber abuse, cyberbullying of children, or the livestreaming of violent or other harmful content," the advice said.

"The harms linked to covert recording are not hypothetical. They are real and already occurring."

Among the concerns listed by the commissioner was how the glasses could be used by "pick-up artists" who use the glasses to film women without their knowledge.

"Most of the women do not realise they are being filmed. These posts often attract misogynistic comments, compounding the harm," the commissioner said.

"Used in this way, smart glasses can reinforce and normalise watching, recording and controlling women in public without their knowledge."

The commissioner has also called for livestreaming from the glasses to operate on a delay, as well as for recording to be disabled when the glasses are not being worn.

Attorney-General Michelle Rowland wrote to the privacy commission earlier this month to investigate whether extra regulations for smart glasses were needed.

The Greens have called for a 12 month ban on the importation of smart glasses.

Under changes the minor party will bring to parliament, the filming, storing or sharing of footage from the glasses without consent would be a breach of privacy laws.

Social media and deletion requests

Rowland is also set to outline further changes to privacy laws, including the right to erasure, on Monday.

The policy would mean social media users can ask tech companies to delete their personal information published online or held by the platforms.

The draft laws will not apply to media organisations publishing news articles.

Rowland said the privacy laws were needed to keep up with technology changes.

"The right to erasure will help put more control in the hands of Australians, allowing personal information to be destroyed from large digital platforms," she said.

"We must ensure appropriate safeguards are placed around technology and stop the erosion of our privacy protections."

The federal government will also roll out extra protections for identity documents online.

A service called IDLock will allow people to block or unblock the use of identity documents such as passports.

IDLock will be made available through the government's MyGov platform from 2027 after a small-scale trial in late 2026.

"Australians deserve to have control over how their personal identity information, such as their driver licence or passport, is used to verify their identity online," Rowland said.

"As data breaches, scams and cyber-enabled crime continue to evolve, Australia's approach must evolve with them."

title: Australian boxing great Tony Mundine dies aged 75
text:
In brief Australian boxing legend Tony Mundine has died aged 75.

Mundine presided over a three-generation boxing dynasty including son Anthony and grandson Rahim.

Indigenous Australian boxing great Tony Mundine has died, aged 75.

The father of former boxer and NRL star Anthony Mundine succumbed to a heart attack on Sunday.

Born in Baryulgil, near Grafton in northern NSW, Tony Mundine was the first Australian to fight in four different weight divisions, challenging for the world middleweight title against Argentina's Carlos Monzon in 1974, in a bout stopped in the seventh round.

Mundine leaves a significant boxing legacy. Anthony was an IBO middleweight and WBA super-middleweight world champion, whose son Rahim won his fourth career fight from as many professional bouts on the Gold Coast only last week.

It was an action-packed morning at Alan Jones’ criminal trial in the Downing Centre Local Court in Sydney.

If you’re just joining us now, Jones’ long-time talkback colleague at 2GB, Ray Hadley, returned to the witness box today after a brief stint on Tuesday.

Ray Hadley arrives at court on Wednesday. Dominic Lorrimer

Hadley has given evidence that complainant “C”, one of six men who has accused Jones of unwanted touching and kissing, confided in him in late 2019 about the alleged indecent assaults. Jones denies the allegations.

Hadley is now being cross-examined by Jones’ barrister Gabrielle Bashir, SC. She is expected to put to him that he encouraged “C” to make the allegations about Jones because the two broadcasters were professional rivals, but she has yet to launch this line of questioning.

Hadley revealed during his cross-examination that he signed a “secret contract” in late 2018 to take over Jones’ breakfast radio slot at 2GB from July 2019, after he was approached by John Singleton.

Singleton was then a major shareholder in Macquarie Media, the company that owned 2GB.

He said the deal fell over when Singleton sold down his stake in Macquarie Media to Nine Entertainment, the owner of this masthead, but that he insisted 2GB honour the agreement to double his salary from $2 million to $4 million.

Nine has since sold its radio division, and Hadley retired from the airwaves in 2024.

Hadley denied that he regarded the breakfast slot as the pinnacle of professional achievement and said he was motivated by money when he signed the deal.

He denied that it was a difficult time for him when Jones re-signed his contract for two years in May 2019, saying: “Inadvertently Mr Jones had doubled my salary for doing the same job.”

Hadley told the court that a 2GB employee told him in about 2019 that Alan Jones had “marshalled the troops and said, ‘dig up some dirt on Hadley’.” Bashir asked if he had come to court to discredit that 2GB employee. “Not at all, I’ve come here to tell the truth, I’m under oath,” Hadley responded.

Hadley has agreed that he called Jones many derogatory names over the years, and said they had a “tumultuous relationship”. He was taken to a text exchange he had with Jones in 2019 when Jones was sick. Jones had said he had been “crook as Rookwood”, in a reference to the Sydney cemetery. Hadley had joked in response that he loved Jones “above ground”.

The missing family were checked into the now-destroyed Kailash Hotel, but Kowshikan believes they may well have been elsewhere when the flood struck.

title: Clarkson speaks after North Melbourne sack him with a year to run on contract
text:
Advertisement

North Melbourne have sacked coach Alastair Clarkson after four seasons and with a year remaining on his contract. Players and staff were called into the club for an emergency meeting on Wednesday morning, weeks after the end of their men’s season. Loading Two people with knowledge of the meeting, who spoke on condition of anonymity, confirmed that it was about Clarkson’s future, and members of a coterie group were informed by the club that the 58-year-old would not coach the Roos in 2027. Clarkson was told of the club’s decision on Tuesday after a post-season consultation period during which North bosses sought the views of the football department and players, two sources confirmed.

Advertisement

The leadership’s view, as communicated to the coterie, was that the Kangaroos had made progress under Clarkson but felt they needed to extract more from a talented group. Clarkson issued a statement via his management. Alastair Clarkson is leaving North Melbourne. Getty Images “My time as coach of the North Melbourne Football Club has come to an end,” he said. “We set out to stabilise the club and lay the foundations for a return to playing deep in September.

Advertisement

“The challenge was a difficult one that I embraced with my whole being. “My family and I have been privileged to be involved in AFL football for over 40 years, but it is now time for a new chapter.” Clarkson, who coached Hawthorn to four premierships before departing at the end of the 2020 season, has been with the Kangaroos since his appointment in late 2022. The Roos finished 14th this year with nine wins and 14 losses. They had been in the top 10 with eight wins on June 21 but slumped out of finals contention since.

Advertisement

It was their highest result under Clarkson after finishes of 17th in his first two years in charge and 16th in 2025. “We asked Alastair to give our club stability and strength and help return us to the top of the AFL ladder,” club president Sonja Hood said. “Four years later, we have created an environment where our staff and players want to be at our club. This is a testament to the culture Alastair has helped create and the belief that he has built in this group. “Although we have clearly made progress and won more games, we won’t shy away from our desire to want more from this talented group.

Advertisement

“We are incredibly grateful to Alastair for the work he’s done over the last four years and we wish him all the very best for his next chapter.” Related Article AFL 2026 ‘This is on me, not the club’: Alastair Clarkson opens up on the Roos’ plight Viney, Clarkson’s longtime lieutenant and friend, will remain at the club and is expected to be part of the coach search process. North Melbourne players were spotted emerging from the Roos’ facilities at Arden Street after the meeting but would not comment beyond expressing excitement for next season. As previously reported by this masthead, Clarkson signed a five-year deal worth more than $5 million when he agreed to return to his former club and has a contract that essentially guarantees him the full amount of his 2027 contract, according to sources with knowledge of the deal.

Advertisement

North Melbourne, who have received the highest amount of variable funding from the AFL of Victorian clubs over the past two years (surpassing St Kilda who had long held that mantle), have been a relatively frugal club since the 2000s. The Roos wiped off their debt and enjoyed repeated financial benefits from their stint of playing home games in Hobart and now Western Australia. External discussion of Clarkson’s position and future has included the fact that Adam Simpson and John Longmire – both Kangaroos playing greats who went on to coach AFL premierships at other clubs – are not presently employed as senior coaches. Other potential targets could include Corey Enright and Jaymie Graham, who were contenders for the Carlton and Essendon jobs, respectively, before Josh Fraser and Mark McVeigh were appointed by those clubs. Loading In March, Clarkson told this masthead he was all for someone else taking the top job at North Melbourne if they were better placed for a quicker return to premiership contention.

Advertisement

“I came back here to help the footy club. [It’s] nothing to do with ego, nothing to do with anything else except repay to North what they gave to me as a young fellow,” he said. North had not guaranteed Clarkson’s position when pressed on whether he would coach in 2027 as contracted. Western Bulldogs coach Luke Beveridge was shocked when he was told of Clarkson’s fate midway through his press conference on Wednesday. “Really?” Beveridge said. “Jeez.” Beveridge served as an assistant coach under Clarkson at Hawthorn in 2012-14 when the Hawks won two flags and were narrowly beaten by Sydney in a grand final.

Advertisement

Related Article AFL 2026 Clarkson’s clause: Frugal Roos would face huge payout if they axed coach early The Dogs coach said the constant scrutiny on senior coaches right from the start of their tenure was “disconcerting”, even if he accepted it came with the territory. “The difficult thing with what we’re all doing is it’s a different culture now in our code,” Beveridge said. “We’ve almost become like the EPL where senior coaches’ tenure and your own coaching mortality is speculated about a lot more than it used to be, as opposed to say the NFL, where you can have a winning season and that’s considered a success. “What I’m concerned about is the next generation of senior coaches. Do they actually really want to put them in the situation where, from the start of their tenure, their vocational sustainability is speculated upon? It’s not a nice place to live.”

Advertisement

Beveridge paid tribute to Clarkson’s coaching career. “Clarko’s been an amazing coach, amazing custodian of the game, and obviously really outspoken, and someone who’s pushed his own opinions to make the game better,” Beveridge said. text:

Updated SportTennisUS Open From GoFundMe to making big bank: Australian’s US Open breakthrough Marc McGowan Updated September 2, 2026 — 12:58pm ,first published 11:19am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Dane Sweeny created a GoFundMe account as a teenager to beg for money to keep his tennis dream alive. That is now just a distant memory for the happy-go-lucky Australian as he closes in on his top-100 debut after winning his second match at a grand slam on Wednesday (AEST) at the US Open – and first away from Melbourne Park. Dane Sweeny is into the second round at the US Open for the first time. Getty Images Sweeny, now 25, advanced to the second round when zany Frenchman Corentin Moutet retired with an arm injury while trailing Australia’s world No.123 by a 7-6 (7-4), 6-4, 3-0 scoreline on a rain-interrupted day in New York that delayed play by almost four hours. Two further delays, and a gloomy forecast, eventually convinced tournament officials to stop play for the night on the outside courts.

Advertisement

Related Article US Open Four Aussies dropped their first sets at the US Open. What followed were four brilliant comebacks That decision pushed Australia’s leading hope and No.6 seed Alex de Minaur’s opening match against 187th-ranked Italian qualifier Andrea Guerrieri onto Thursday’s schedule (AEST). Sweeny will pocket almost $266,000 prizemoney, on top of the roughly $560,000 he had already earned in a career-best year to date, including winning a round at the Australian Open and qualifying for Wimbledon. Australia will have at least seven players in the second round, with Tristan Schoolkate following his close friend Sweeny in winning on Wednesday before the rain returned. Schoolkate beat fellow qualifier Nishesh Basavareddy 7-6 (7-4), 3-6, 6-3, 6-4 to reach this stage at Flushing Meadows for the third year in a row.

Advertisement

“It’s really nice. I’m always rooting for the Aussie boys, and it’s nice to see a couple get over the line, especially Tristan,” Sweeny said. “We’ve known each other for so long.” Schoolkate was similarly thrilled for Sweeny, saying they were “amped” to see each other at the start of the day and that he spent his match with one eye on the scoreboard tracking his friend’s progress. Loading The draw gets tougher from here for both players, with highly ranked Italians Lorenzo Musetti and Flavio Cobolli up next for Sweeny and Schoolkate, respectively. “I’m really excited to play Musetti,” Sweeny said.

Advertisement

“It’s going to be a great match. He’s obviously one of the world’s best players, and I’m really excited to take it to him.” Moutet was up to his usual tricks against Sweeny, demolishing a racquet – which he later gifted to a fan – mockingly blowing a kiss to the sky after an ace, and double-faulting at 4-4 in the second set on his way to conceding a costly break. Schoolkate has made the second round in New York three years running. Getty Images He had clearly had enough by the time he dropped serve a second time in the third set, although he did have strapping on his left arm throughout the match. Sweeny, who is listed at 170 centimetres on the ATP website, was due to contest US Open qualifying until a series of withdrawals enabled Alexei Popyrin to make the main draw off his ranking, which opened Tennis Australia’s reciprocal wildcard for Sweeny.

Advertisement

Australia’s top-ranked woman, Daria Kasatkina, was on the brink of defeat when rain put her opener against Spain’s former world No.2 Paula Badosa on hold for a second time, trailing 6-1, 5-4, with Badosa serving for the match and two points from the win. However, injury-cursed Thanasi Kokkinakis pulled out of his scheduled clash with another Spaniard, rising star Rafael Jodar, because of an ankle setback. Loading Among the other stars to progress on Wednesday were 2024 champion Coco Gauff – who will face Badosa or Kasatkina – world No.2 Elena Rybakina, Mirra Andreeva, Madison Keys and Taylor Fritz, but 12th seed Belinda Bencic lost in three sets to Yulia Putintseva. Retiring French entertainer Gael Monfils also won on his 40th birthday, downing Paraguay’s Adolfo Daniel Vallejo 2-6, 6-1, 6-2, 6-0.

title: Coles and Woolworths drop krill supplements
text:

Breaking EnvironmentSustainabilitySupermarkets Coles and Woolworths drop krill supplements Caitlin Fitzsimmons September 2, 2026 — 12:36pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Coles and Woolworths have stopped selling nutritional supplements made from krill, a tiny crustacean that is the major food source for iconic Antarctic wildlife such as Emperor penguins and whales. The supermarket giants confirmed the decision in response to questions from this masthead but both declined to comment further. Krill supplements, taken as a source of Omega-3 fatty acids, are still sold in smaller retailers and most pharmacies. A humpback whale fluking in front of a krill super trawler last summer. Sea Shepherd The withdrawal by Coles and Woolworths comes amid an international campaign by environmental groups to try to curb the burgeoning krill fishing industry because of fears about the pressure on the Antarctic ecosystem. Captain Peter Hammarstedt, director of campaigns at Sea Shepherd Global, drew attention to the Coles move with a LinkedIn post, noting that international retailers UK-based Holland & Barrett and German retailers dm-drogerie markt and Dirk Rossmann GmbH had also withdrawn from the market.

Advertisement

Antarctic krill is the keystone species of the Southern Ocean. Brett Wilks / AAPP “We have already seen market forces begin to shift decisively away from krill in the United Kingdom and Germany,” Hammarstedt said. “Now that change has reached Australian shores.” Holland & Barrett, a health food chain with more than 1000 stores in Britain, helped cofound the Antarctic Krill Pledge, which has since been signed by a number of smaller retailers. Krill-based nutritional supplements are currently worth an estimated $US110.1 million ($154.01 million) globally, according to Future Market Insights, and this is expected to grow to $US216.59 million by 2036, driven largely by demand in China and North America.

Advertisement

The sustainability claims on a bottle of red krill supplements. Audrey Richardson In Australia, krill oil is the fastest-growing source segment within Australia’s Omega-3 supplements market, Complementary Medicines Australia said. Sea Shepherd Global has spent the past few Antarctic summers documenting the krill fishing in Antarctica to raise public awareness, and supporting scientists to study the ecological effects but without trying to prevent operations since krill fishing is a legal activity under international agreements. Captain Paul Watson Foundation took a different approach and engaged in direct action to try to disrupt the krill harvest as much as possible. The rapid increase in the size of the krill fishing fleet over the past few years meant that last month the krill fishery closed early for the second year in a row. The fishery reached its catch limit of 620,000 tonnes and automatically closed on August 12, months ahead of schedule. Emperor penguins rely on sea ice for breeding and as a source of krill. LightRocket via Getty Images

Advertisement

Krill fishing nations such as Norway are pushing to double the catch limit to 1.2 million tonnes, though they are unlikely to secure the international consensus needed to change the rules.
